q:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Adults who consistently sleep fewer than seven hours a night face measurably higher risks of obesity, high blood pressure, and heart disease. During deep sleep, the brain clears metabolic waste, consolidates memories, and regulates hormones that control hunger. People who are sleep deprived produce more ghrelin, the hormone that signals hunger, and less leptin, the hormone that signals fullness — a combination that drives overeating. The good news is that the damage is partly reversible: extending sleep by even one hour a night improves attention, mood, and blood sugar control within weeks. Sleep, in short, is not lost time; it is maintenance the body cannot skip.

Dehydration can impair thinking long before a person feels thirsty. Even a fluid loss of one to two percent of body weight — easily reached during a busy hospital shift — reduces concentration, slows reaction time, and increases headache frequency.
